passages.t: A faith as precious as ours
passages.happening: “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
The writer names himself ‘Simon Peter’, both his Jewish name and the name Jesus gave him. He is ‘a servant and apostle’, under orders and sent.

He writes to people who have received ‘a faith as precious as ours’. The apostles had walked with Jesus; these readers had not. But their faith is not second-rate. It is of equal worth, because it rests on the same righteousness of the same Lord.

That Lord is called ‘our God and Savior Jesus Christ’. In the Greek, the grammar most naturally applies both titles, ‘God’ and ‘Savior’, to Jesus. It is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is God.

Then a word that runs through the whole letter: ‘knowledge’. The Greek word means full, personal knowledge, knowing someone, not only knowing about them. Grace and peace grow as believers come to know God and Jesus better. Some teachers in these churches seem to have claimed a special, secret knowledge. Peter says real knowledge is of a person, and it bears fruit.

The question of who wrote this letter is a real one, and the book page sets out the main views. These notes call the writer ‘Peter’, as the letter does.
passages.ot:
Calling the Lord ‘our God and Savior’ uses the language Israel used of the LORD: “For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior” (Isaiah 43:3).

And ‘grace and peace’ gathers up Israel's old blessing: “may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:25-26).
passages.asks: Ask whether you think of your faith as lesser than the faith of the great saints. Ask what it would mean to know Jesus better this year, not only to know more about him. And ask what it means to call him ‘our God and Savior’.

passages.t: Everything we need, and making every effort
passages.happening:
“His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires” (verses 3-4).

“For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love” (verses 5-7).

“For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins. Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (verses 8-11).
passages.hearers:
Peter starts with what God has done. His power has already given ‘everything we need for life and godliness’. Nothing essential is missing.

Then a bold promise: believers ‘become partakers of the divine nature’. Some of this language had echoes in Greek religion, but Peter's meaning is shaped by God's promises and by escaping the world's corruption, not by losing the self in God (see below).

Then comes ‘for this very reason’. Because God has given so much, make every effort. Peter builds a ladder, each step added to the one before. Greek moral teachers loved lists of virtues, and some of these words were theirs: ‘virtue’, ‘self-control’, ‘godliness’. But Peter's ladder starts with faith and ends with love, and God's power drives it. It is a form also used by Paul (Romans 5:3-5).

The opposite of growth is a kind of blindness. A person who stops growing becomes ‘nearsighted’, seeing only what is close, and forgets the cleansing he has received.

‘Make your calling and election sure’ (see below). Peter promises that those who grow ‘will never stumble’ and will be welcomed lavishly into Christ's kingdom. The picture is of a warm, generous welcome home.
passages.ot:
Peter's promises echo God's promise that his people will reflect him. Humanity was made in God's image from the start: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

The growing life is the psalm's tree: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season” (Psalm 1:3). And it is the path of Proverbs: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday” (Proverbs 4:18).
passages.hard:
What does it mean to ‘become partakers of the divine nature’? And how can anyone ‘make your calling and election sure’?

The first phrase is one of the boldest in the New Testament. Orthodox teaching draws on it for theosis, union with God by grace, in which believers share God's life without ever ceasing to be creatures. Western churches usually read it as sharing God's holy character and his undying life through union with Christ. All agree that it does not mean becoming God in essence. These notes do not choose.

The second phrase is read in line with Christians' wider views of God's choosing. Reformed Christians read it as confirming in life what God has already done: growth is the evidence of his call, not the cause of it. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read it as a call to persevere in a calling that can be abandoned. Both agree that Peter is not asking anyone to earn God's choice, and that he writes to give assurance: ‘you will never stumble’. These notes do not choose.

If you are afraid that you are not chosen, hear the invitation of Jesus: “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Read the ladder of verses 5 to 7 slowly. Ask which step you most need to add. Ask where you have become nearsighted, forgetting what God has done for you. And ask whether you are growing, or standing still.

passages.happening: “Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have. I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times” (verses 12-15).
passages.hearers:
This is the voice of a farewell. Peter's readers already know the truth. He is not bringing new teaching. He is reminding them, so that they will remember after he is gone. ‘Remind’, ‘refresh your memory’, ‘recall’: the words come three times in four verses.

He calls his body ‘a tent’. A tent is a home for travellers, put up for a while and then taken down. It may recall Israel's tents in the wilderness, or the shelters Peter once offered to build on the mountain of the transfiguration (Mark 9:5).

‘As our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me.’ After the resurrection, Jesus told Peter how he would die (John 21:18-19). If Peter wrote this, he is near that death now. Early tradition says he died in Rome under Nero.

The letter as a whole takes the form of a farewell testament, a kind of writing in which a leader facing death passes on what matters most. Those who think the letter was written after Peter's death in his name see the form as a way of keeping his teaching for a new generation. Those who hold that Peter wrote it see a real man saying his last words. The book page sets out both.
passages.ot:
The Bible has other farewells like this. God told Moses, “Behold, the time of your death is near. Call Joshua and present yourselves at the Tent of Meeting, so that I may commission him” (Deuteronomy 31:14). And Joshua said to Israel at the end of his life, “today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed” (Joshua 23:14).

Israel remembered its wilderness tents every year at the Feast of Booths: “You are to dwell in booths for seven days” (Leviticus 23:42).
passages.hard:
If the letter was written after Peter's death, in his name, would that make it dishonest? And can it still be Scripture?

Christians who hold that Peter wrote it see no problem: these are his own last words. Christians and scholars who think a follower wrote it after his death answer the question in different ways. Some hold that a farewell testament written in a famous teacher's name was a known form of writing, and that the first readers may have recognised it for what it was, a faithful setting-down of the teacher's message for a new day, not a forgery meant to deceive. Others find that hard to square with the letter's personal claims, such as being on the mountain (1:18), and that is one reason they hold that Peter wrote it.

The early church took the question seriously. It rejected other writings that carried Peter's name, such as the Gospel of Peter, and after long discussion it received this one. These notes do not choose who held the pen. With the church, they receive the letter as Scripture, and they read it as God's word to us.
passages.asks: Ask what you would want to pass on if you knew your time was short. Ask whether you need to be reminded of things you already know, and who reminds you. And ask how you can help the people who come after you remember.

passages.t: Eyewitnesses, and the word of the prophets
passages.happening:
“For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (verses 16-18).

“We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (verses 19-21).
passages.hearers:
Some were saying that the apostles' message about Christ's coming in power was a myth. ‘Fables’ is the word for myths, like the stories of the Greek gods, which many educated people of the time thought were poetic inventions. Peter answers: we did not make it up. We saw.

He points to the transfiguration. The Gospels tell how Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain and was changed before them, and a voice spoke from the cloud. The Gospels do not name the mountain. Later tradition named Mount Tabor in Galilee, and some modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon. Peter calls it ‘the holy mountain’ because of what happened there. That glimpse of glory was, for him, a preview of Christ's coming in power.

‘Eyewitness’ was the strongest kind of evidence in ancient law and in history writing.

Then a second witness: the prophets. Their word is like a lamp in a dark place. A lamp does not light the whole world, but it shows the way until morning. ‘The morning star’ most likely means Christ himself, whose coming brings the full day.

The last two verses say how prophecy came. Not ‘by the will of man’, but people spoke from God ‘as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit’. The same verb is used in Acts of a ship driven by the wind. The prophets were moved by the Spirit and still spoke as themselves, in their own words.
passages.ot:
The Father's words echo two Old Testament passages: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7), and “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights” (Isaiah 42:1).

The star echoes Balaam's prophecy: “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17). The lamp echoes a psalm: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).

And the prophets themselves said where their words came from: “The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue” (2 Samuel 23:2). Jeremiah warned against prophets who “speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16).
passages.hard:
What does ‘no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation’ mean?

It can be read two main ways. These notes do not choose. On the first, it is about where prophecy came from: the prophets did not produce their messages from their own reading of events, because, as verse 21 says, they spoke from God as the Spirit carried them. Many interpreters favour this reading because it fits the next verse.

On the second, it is about how prophecy is read: no one should interpret Scripture alone or by private whim, but with the Spirit's help and within the community of faith. Catholic and Orthodox teaching has often drawn on this reading in support of the church's teaching office. Protestant teaching stresses that Scripture is its own best interpreter.

The two are not wholly opposed. If prophecy comes from God, it must be read as God's word, not bent to our purposes. All agree that Scripture must not be twisted to suit ourselves, as Peter warns again in 3:16.
passages.asks: Ask what your faith rests on: a feeling, a tradition, or the witness of people who saw. Ask how you treat Scripture, as a lamp to walk by or as a book to bend to your wishes. And ask whether the morning star has risen in your heart.
